summary: Updates the H ratio from RFC 1715 and defines a new ratio, which the authors say is easier to understand, for measuring how efficiently addresses are assigned.

eli5.summary: It's a score for how well you use up a pile of numbered seats.

questions: what is the h ratio for address assignment
how do you measure address allocation efficiency
what is a good hd ratio
subtitle: A logarithm-based score for how full an address space is, replacing the H ratio with a 0 to 100 percent scale.

tldr.problem: The H ratio from RFC 1715 gives values like 0.25 on a scale that tops out at 0.30103, which people found hard to explain.
tldr.mechanism: The HD-ratio is the logarithm of allocated objects divided by the logarithm of the maximum allocatable objects, giving a value from 0 to 1 that is shown as a percentage.
tldr.outcome: Worked examples suggest about 80 percent is a comfortable level and 85 percent and above is painful, which lets the authors estimate practical capacity for address plans.

today: RFC 3194 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 1715. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Address Use Is Not Linear
sections.content:
It is tempting to think a 10-digit phone plan numbers 10 billion telephones, or that 32-bit IPv4 addresses number 4 billion computers. The RFC says this is wrong: the 10-digit plan is stressed with a few hundred million telephones in North America, and Internet registries tightened their policies when there were only a few tens of million computers.

Addressing plans are hierarchies, with margins left at every level for growth and mobility. When the margin runs out, renumbering is painful and expensive. Inefficiency also multiplies across levels: 50% efficiency at each stage of a three-level hierarchy gives 12.5% overall. So a useful "pain level indicator" has to account for that.
sections.eli5: When you leave spare seats at every table, the empty seats add up. A good score has to notice how crowded things get, not just count the people.

sections.title: From the H Ratio to the HD-Ratio
sections.content:
The H-Ratio in RFC 1715 is the base 10 logarithm of the number of allocated addresses divided by the address size in bits. It does not depend on address size, but its values run from 0.0 to 0.30103, with typical values from 0.20 to 0.28. The authors found these numbers hard to explain.

This memo introduces the Host Density ratio, or HD-Ratio, as a proposed replacement. Its values run from 0 to 1 and are usually given as percentages, which the authors believe is easier to understand and more expressive.
sections.eli5: The old score ran from 0 to about 0.3, which is confusing. The new one runs from 0 to 100 percent, like a school grade.

sections.title: The HD-Ratio Formula
sections.content:
The ratio is defined as HD = log(allocated objects) / log(maximum allocatable objects). It applies when the maximum is greater than 1 and the number allocated is at least 1 and no more than the maximum. It is 0% with a single allocation and 100% when every available address has an object. Any logarithm base works as long as both parts use the same one.

In most cases it can be derived from the H ratio as HD = H / log10(2).
sections.eli5: Take the size of your crowd and the size of the whole street, squash both with a logarithm, and divide. Full means 100 percent.

sections.title: Using HD as a Pain Indicator
sections.content:
RFC 1715 looked at networks that reached their capacity limit, on the idea that managers delay renumbering until it is too painful. The RFC recomputes these as HD values:

  • French telephone numbers at 8 digits with 1.0E+7 phones: 87.5%. At 9 digits: 77.8%.
  • US telephone numbers at "9.2" digits with 1.0E+8 subscribers: 87.0%. At 10 digits: 80.0%.
  • DECnet Phase IV stopped growing at about 15K nodes in a 16-bit address space: 86.7%.

The direct quotients for the three cases were 10%, 3.2% and 22.8%, which do not generalize, while the HD values are close. The authors conclude that about 85% and above is a high pain level, and that values of 80% or less after renumbering suggest a comfortable trade-off.
sections.eli5: Different towns all ran out of room at about the same crowded score. That tells us the score is a good warning light.

sections.title: Estimating Capacity
sections.content:
Reversing the formula gives the number of objects that can be allocated: (maximum allocatable objects)^HD. The RFC tabulates results for different pain levels, with 1M meaning 1,000,000.

It stresses that the practical maximum depends on how much pain users and providers will accept, and that more than 154M allocated IPv4 addresses may well happen if that pain is accepted. The memo states it has no security implications and requests no IANA action.
sections.eli5: You can run the score backwards to ask how many people fit before the street feels too crowded. It depends on how crowded you are willing to be.

references.text: Huitema, C., "The H Ratio for Address Assignment Efficiency", RFC 1715, November 1994.
